He sleeps in a big old wooden dog house.
Walking all three of them is exhausting.
By eight in the morning I am exhausted.
Something just walked across your camera. Was that a dog? How many do you have?
Three. All rescues, all mutts, and not one of them was planned.
One is a big boisterous young thing who never stops moving. One is a docile old lady who sleeps through everything. And the third is a small scruffy brown one who was the runt of the litter.
Are they friendly? I only ask because my sister’s dog is wary of new people and it took me two whole years.
The little one is wary of everybody. The other two are so clingy it is embarrassing. I fuss over them far too much, honestly.
Nothing wrong with that. Do the three of them get along?
Most of the time. There is an old argument between the two youngest that nobody has ever solved, so we let sleeping dogs lie.

The first time I saw her she was a small scruffy grey thing sitting outside the bakery in the rain. A stray, obviously. Nobody in my village wanted her, because she was the runt of the litter and everybody assumed she would not survive the winter. So I took her home. That was eleven years ago. She is a mutt, she has no pedigree at all, and she is the most stubborn animal I have ever met. For the first two months she was wary of everybody, my husband included. She would not come near the kitchen. And then one morning she simply decided that we were hers, and since that day she has been unbearably clingy. If I go to another room, she follows me. If I sit down, she is on my feet. My mother says I fuss over that dog more than I ever fussed over my brothers, and honestly, she is right.

People always ask me which one is easier, and the honest answer is neither, for completely opposite reasons. Cooper is a big boisterous two year old retriever who has never walked calmly anywhere in his life. Taking him out is exhausting. By the time we get back I am exhausted and he is only getting started. Then there is Maple, who is nine, completely docile, and would sleep through an earthquake. The vet calls her the easy one. The problem is that she barely moves, so I have to talk her into every single walk. She only perks up when she hears the leash, and even then it takes about a minute. My wife says the two of them together would make one perfect dog, split into two animals. She is not wrong. I would not trade either of them, although some mornings I do think about it.
